title: Soft tentacle gripper
summary: Four pneumatic silicone tentacles that wrap around fragile, irregular produce — designed in hyperelastic FEA, cast in 3D-printed molds and built into a working 2-DOF robot.
role: Team of 5 · FEA, mold design & casting

cover.alt: The assembled tentacle gripper prototype on a lab bench

tldr: I owned the tentacle: chamber geometry in FEA, the casting mold and the 3D-printed tooling.
Silicone modeled as a 2nd-order Ogden hyperelastic material; geometry chosen in simulation before printing any tooling.
The team integrated it on a 2-DOF arm with belt reductions, an Arduino-controlled pneumatic circuit and a public build guide.
facts: Tentacle FEA, casting mold design, 3D-printed tooling
Ayoub Hamam, Julian Meskens, Matteo Paolini, Ariadne Samaey, Henri Wauthier
Mechatronics project, VUB / ULB Brussels — supervised by Prof. Bram Vanderborght

sections.title: The problem
body: Fruit sorting is still largely manual because produce is delicate and every piece has a different shape. Rigid grippers either damage it or need a custom tool per product. The brief: a low-cost soft gripper that can pick up a small fruit (200 g) safely, on a simple robot arm.

sections.title: Designing the tentacle in simulation
body: Each tentacle is a silicone finger with internal air chambers. When pressurized, the thin side stretches more than the thick side and the finger curls around the object. Getting enough curvature at a low, safe pressure depends on the chamber geometry — so I worked it out in FEA before printing anything.

list: Material: Dragon Skin 20 silicone, modeled in ANSYS Workbench as a second-order Ogden hyperelastic material (incompressible, 1070 kg/m³).
Boundary conditions: tentacle base fixed, internal pressure applied in steps on the chamber walls.
Design iteration: three chamber layouts (mk2 → mk3 → mk4) simulated with the same material model and loads, compared on how the finger bends.

sections.title: From model to cast part
body: Silicone parts are only as good as their mold. I designed a two-part PLA mold with a removable core that forms the air channel. The halves are screwed together so they can be opened without tearing the part and reused for every tentacle; compressed air breaks the seal between silicone and core during demolding.

body.caption: Technical drawing of the casting mold and core.

sections.title: The full robot
body: The team integrated four tentacles on a gripper hub mounted on a 2-DOF arm. A torque analysis showed the shoulder needed 2.40 N·m — more than the MG996R servos can deliver directly — so the arm uses belt reductions of 4 and 1.5. An Arduino switches the pump and valves through MOSFETs.

sections.title: Results and what I'd do next
body: The prototype grasps and lifts the target objects with the four tentacles — a working proof of concept of the design.

The team's critical review found the shoulder not stiff enough, the custom timing belts unreliable, and no active pump regulation. On my side, the next step is a pressure–bending test rig to compare the cast tentacle with the FEA and fit the Ogden parameters to the real part.
